title: Pete Golding to Ole Miss fans: ‘Don’t lose what we’ve created’ by crossing the line with Lane Kiffin
content:
OXFORD, Miss. — Ole Miss is known as one of the most hospitable places in college football for visiting fans. But the person — and team — the Rebels dislike the most will be in town Saturday.

So Ole Miss coach Pete Golding took the opportunity Monday to preach restraint when asked whether he had a message for the fans. Their vitriol for LSU coach Lane Kiffin, the man who left the Rebels amid last year’s College Football Playoff run to coach a rival, will be expressed loudly on Saturday when No. 7 LSU (2-0) takes on No. 8 Ole Miss (2-0).

That’s expected and appreciated. Anything beyond loud noise is discouraged, and perhaps feared by those in charge at Ole Miss, given how emotional Kiffin’s return will be.

“To me, what this place has always been about, why so many people love coming here and respect this place is because of the people who are here and how they make (opposing fans) feel when they come here,” said Golding, who is in his first full season as Ole Miss coach after serving as Kiffin’s defensive coordinator. “Be there early and be loud. But I think at the end of the day, there’s still a respect piece. And this place has always been known to have really, really good people. Let’s not lose that over a game or a person or anything like that.”

Added Golding, “At the end of the day, don’t lose what we’ve created.”

LSU fans will be part of the atmosphere as well, of course, and the mixing of those two fan bases has created contentious moments before — long before Kiffin was part of the Magnolia Bowl rivalry. He takes it to a new level.

Kiffin’s departure, and failed attempt to continue coaching Ole Miss in the Playoff despite taking the LSU job, and public comments at Ole Miss’ expense, and poaching of four former Ole Miss players who followed him to LSU, and attempt to bring Ole Miss star quarterback Trinidad Chambliss with him, all factor into the hard feelings.

Kiffin is well aware, of course, and told reporters Monday that LSU has discussed the environment that awaits.

“I guess there’s real safety issues and stuff, so there’s people that have a plan for that,” Kiffin said. “I told the players today, ‘Man, you don’t have anything to worry about as far as, like, attention on you all week and everything. There’s going to be so much attention, hatred, everything on me. You just get to go play. Really, the pressure’s on them. They’re the team that — we won seven games last year. They won 13. They return two Heisman candidates. How often does that ever happen in the same backfield? We had it one time (at USC) with Matt Leinart and Reggie Bush … You guys just get to go play. The pressure’s not on you.’”

Throw in the magnitude of the game, the presence of ESPN’s “College GameDay” and a massive media presence for what has been dubbed the game of the year in college football, and Golding also has to worry about his own players maintaining focus and emotional control.

“It’s like high school homecoming,” he said. “You focus on the wrong s—, that homecoming dance isn’t so good if you got beat on Friday night.”

— Matt Baker contributed reporting.
